description: Carnegie Vanguard Hackathon Club Main Team
summary:
Terra is a web platform that answers plain-language questions about how the ground is changing, anywhere on Earth. A user picks a place and asks, for example, "What changed on Mount Etna, and which polarization shows it?" Terra finds matching NASA–ISRO NISAR radar passes, reads only that area from the original products, and measures calibrated backscatter change in both co- and cross-polarization. It shows the result on a 3D globe and writes an answer in which every number is checked against a computed value.
 Radar sees through cloud and darkness, but it measures how much the ground changed, not what changed. Terra closes that gap. Each changed patch becomes a testable hypothesis: rougher ground, new water or vegetation loss. Autonomous drones, flown here on real ArduPilot firmware in simulation, are sent to check each one. Every observation is judged against Sentinel-2, land-cover and thermal data, and the results flow into one traceable report.
 This turns NISAR's global, all-weather coverage into verified answers that disaster responders, scientists and land managers can act on
details:
Terra lets anyone ask a plain-language question about how the ground is changing, anywhere on Earth, and answers it with radar from NISAR, the NASA–ISRO L-band mission. A user draws an area and asks something like "Did this wetland flood, and which polarization shows it?" Terra searches the ASF and Earthdata archive for a compatible pair of passes on the same track, frame and direction. It reads only the user's area from the original GCOV products over HTTP byte ranges, never downloading whole files. It then measures calibrated backscatter change in co- and cross-polarization, using automatic, data-driven thresholds rather than fixed cut-offs, and reports which polarization shows each change more clearly. A language model plans the method and writes the answer, but any number or date that doesn't match a computed value is rejected, so every claim traces to a measurement.

Radar shows how much the ground changed, not why, so Terra turns each changed patch into a testable hypothesis such as rougher ground, new water or vegetation loss. A coordinator auctions the patches to a drone fleet, flown here on real ArduPilot autopilot firmware in simulation. Every look from a drone camera is judged against Sentinel-2, ESA WorldCover and Landsat thermal data. The verdicts, including alternative causes like snowmelt, flow into a single traceable report that can be exported as GeoJSON.

The benefit is timing and trust. Radar sees through cloud, smoke and darkness, exactly when optical satellites fail during floods, eruptions and storms. Terra makes NISAR usable by people who aren't radar experts while staying honest about uncertainty, so responders, scientists and land managers get answers they can check and act on.

We built the frontend in TypeScript with React, Vite and CesiumJS for the 3D globe, which can also show Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles and live hazard feeds from NASA FIRMS, EONET, GIBS and USGS. The backend is Python and FastAPI, with NumPy, SciPy, rasterio and h5py doing the radar science. The drone agents run as Temporal workflows, so they survive a crashed worker and pick up where they stopped. The simulated aircraft use ArduPilot SITL and pymavlink, the web app is deployed on Vercel, and the backend is containerised with Docker.

What makes Terra creative is that it closes the loop from satellite to drone and back: observe, form a hypothesis, verify in the field, then report. Along the way we cared about traceability, about clearly labelling simulated flights as simulated, and about honouring every data licence, including using Google's tiles for display only. We also kept all API keys on the server, made the interface work on screens from 360 px wide with no flashing or pulsing animations, and disclose openly where AI was used.
